Loading necessary libraries:

```{r message=F, warning=F}
library(tidyverse)
library(purrr)

```

# Data Collection steps

We have extracted the data sets from the corresponding websites in the \texttt{NHANES.1.R}, \texttt{NHEFS.1.R}, \texttt{NHEFS.2.R}, \texttt{NHEFS.3.R} files that are there in the GitHub repository.

From each of the \texttt{R} file we have one \texttt{.Rdata} files containing the raw data files. We load them in the environment as below.

```{r}
# rm(list = ls())

load("NHEFS_1.Rdata")
load("NHEFS_2.Rdata")
load("NHEFS_3.Rdata")
load("NHANES_1.Rdata")
```

```{r}

NHANES.1 <- NHANES.1 |> mutate(wave = "NHANES.1")
NHEFS.1  <- NHEFS.1  |> mutate(wave = "NHEFS.1")
NHEFS.2  <- NHEFS.2  |> mutate(wave = "NHEFS.2")
NHEFS.3  <- NHEFS.3  |> mutate(wave = "NHEFS.3")

```

# Data Preparation

To ensure a clean data set, we present the data preparation before delving into any of the any EDA or analysis. This portion of the answer pertains to the question mentioned in 1(d): \textbf{Discuss any potential challenges for subsequent analysis based on this exploratory data analysis, including (but not limited to) whether the same type of information is available for each variable at each time point.}

A lot of variables were needed to create, merge, and clean. We painstakingly do them one by one. These would ease up both the EDA and the subsequent analysis.

-   For the \texttt{vital staus} variable, we could not find it in the NHANES.1 data set. We take everyone to be alive. For the others, we create 2 categories: 1 for alive, 3 for dead. We fill the unknown by \texttt{NA}. We also categorize \texttt{traced alive but lost prior to interview period}, or \texttt{traced alive but without direct subject contact} as alive.

    Notably, NHAFES.3 has only alive or dead categories.

```{r}
NHANES.1$vital.st <- 1

NHEFS.1$vital.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$vital.st)
NHEFS.1$vital.st[NHEFS.1$vital.st %in% 4] <- NA
NHEFS.1$vital.st[NHEFS.1$vital.st %in% 5] <- 1

NHEFS.2$vital.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$vital.st)
NHEFS.2$vital.st[NHEFS.2$vital.st %in% 4] <- NA
NHEFS.2$vital.st[NHEFS.2$vital.st %in% c(5,7)] <- 1

```

-   For the \texttt{sex} variable we just mane it numeric for the four data sets.

```{r}
NHANES.1$sex <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$sex)
NHEFS.1$sex <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$sex)
NHEFS.2$sex <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$sex)
NHEFS.3$sex <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$sex)
```

-   For the \texttt{race} variable, we have three main categories: White, Black, and Others. NHANES.1 data do so.

    For the NHEFS, the try to use finer categories for other, breaking it into Asian, Eskimo or American Indian, and others. We merge them for the NHEFS data set to maintain consistency.

```{r}
NHANES.1$race <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$race)

NHEFS.1$vital.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$vital.st)
NHEFS.1 <- NHEFS.1 |> mutate(race = case_when(race == 4            ~ 1,
                                              race == 3            ~ 2,
                                              race %in% c(1, 2, 5) ~ 3))

NHEFS.2$vital.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$vital.st)
NHEFS.2 <- NHEFS.2 |> mutate(race = case_when(race == 4            ~ 1,
                                              race == 3            ~ 2,
                                              race %in% c(1, 2, 5) ~ 3))

NHEFS.3$vital.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$vital.st)
NHEFS.3 <- NHEFS.3 |> mutate(race = case_when(race == 4            ~ 1,
                                              race == 3            ~ 2,
                                              race %in% c(1, 2, 5) ~ 3))

```

-   For the marital status, we create 5 categories: 1 for married, 2 for widowed, 3 for divorced, 4 for separated, and 5 for never married.

    Notably, the NHANES cohort contains a bunch of child population, creating a separate category under 17 (marked by 6).

    We assign \textit{don't know} or \textit{not ascertained} as \texttt{NA}.

```{r}
NHANES.1$mar.st <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$mar.st)
NHANES.1$mar.st <- NHANES.1$mar.st - 1
NHANES.1$mar.st[NHANES.1$mar.st %in% 0] <- 6
NHANES.1$mar.st[NHANES.1$mar.st %in% 8] <- NA

NHEFS.1$mar.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$mar.st)
NHEFS.1$mar.st[NHEFS.1$mar.st %in% c(8,9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$mar.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$mar.st)
NHEFS.2$mar.st[NHEFS.2$mar.st %in% c(8)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$mar.st <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$mar.st)
NHEFS.3$mar.st[NHEFS.3$mar.st %in% c(-7,-8,-9)] <- NA

```

-   We could not find the \texttt{General Health} variable in the NHANES.1 data set. We try to fill this column by the entries from another entry: \textit{Have you been bothered by any illness, bodily disorder, pains, or fears about your health during the past month?}, where the entries are 0 for all the time, 1 for most of the time, 2 for a good bit of time, 3 for some of the time, 4 for a little bit of time, and 5 for none of the time.

    In the NHEFS data sets the categories are 1 for excellent, 2 for very good, 3 for good, 4 for fair, and 5 for poor.

    We map the 6 categories from NHANES to the the NHEFS categories.

```{r}

NHANES.1$gen.hlth <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$gen.hlth)
NHANES.1 <- NHANES.1 |> mutate(gen.hlth = 
                                 case_when(gen.hlth == 5            ~ 1,
                                           gen.hlth == 4            ~ 2,
                                           gen.hlth == 3            ~ 3,
                                           gen.hlth == 2            ~ 4,
                                           gen.hlth %in% c(1, 0) ~ 5))

NHEFS.1$gen.hlth <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$gen.hlth)
NHEFS.1$gen.hlth[NHEFS.1$gen.hlth %in% c(1, 7, 8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$gen.hlth <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$gen.hlth)
NHEFS.2$gen.hlth[NHEFS.2$gen.hlth %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$gen.hlth <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$gen.hlth)
NHEFS.3$gen.hlth[NHEFS.3$gen.hlth %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   For the history of heart attack we do cleaning for the unnecessary variables. Notably, for the NHANES data set, we just have one category: 2 for never had condition.

```{r}
NHANES.1$hist.hrt.att <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$hist.hrt.att)

NHEFS.1$hist.hrt.att <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$hist.hrt.att)
NHEFS.1$hist.hrt.att[NHEFS.1$hist.hrt.att %in% c(8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$hist.hrt.att <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$hist.hrt.att)
NHEFS.2$hist.hrt.att[NHEFS.2$hist.hrt.att %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$hist.hrt.att <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$hist.hrt.att)
NHEFS.3$hist.hrt.att[NHEFS.3$hist.hrt.att %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   History of TIA couldn't be found for NHANES.1 and NHEFS.3. For the other two data sets, we assign \texttt{NA} for the unnecessary information.

```{r}

NHEFS.1$hist.TIA <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$hist.TIA)
NHEFS.1$hist.TIA[NHEFS.1$hist.TIA %in% c(8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$hist.TIA <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$hist.TIA)
NHEFS.2$hist.TIA[NHEFS.2$hist.TIA %in% c(-1, -8, -9, 96)] <- NA

```

-   For the CVA history, we do the same as above. Notably, for the NHANES data set, we just have one category: 2 for never had condition.

```{r}
NHANES.1$hist.CVA <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$hist.CVA)

NHEFS.1$hist.CVA <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$hist.CVA)
NHEFS.1$hist.CVA[NHEFS.1$hist.CVA %in% c(8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$hist.CVA <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$hist.CVA)
NHEFS.2$hist.CVA[NHEFS.2$hist.CVA %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$hist.CVA <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$hist.CVA)
NHEFS.3$hist.CVA[NHEFS.3$hist.CVA %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   We could not find history of arthritis for the NHEFS.3 data set. For the other NHEFS dats sets, we do the similar cleaning.

    For the NHANES, there is two extra category: 3 which refers to \textit{had condition, not present now} and 9 which refers to \textit{had condition, do not know if it is present now}. We assign these categories to the category presenting history of arthritis.

```{r}
NHANES.1$hist.arth <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$hist.arth)
NHANES.1$hist.arth[NHANES.1$hist.arth %in% c(3, 9)] <- 1

NHEFS.1$hist.arth <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$hist.arth)
NHEFS.1$hist.arth[NHEFS.1$hist.arth %in% c(7, 8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$hist.arth <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$hist.arth)
NHEFS.2$hist.arth[NHEFS.2$hist.arth %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   We could not find history of coronary bypass surgery for the NHANES.1 and NHEFS.1 data set. For the others, we do the similar cleaning.

```{r}

NHEFS.2$hist.cor.byp <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$hist.cor.byp)
NHEFS.2$hist.cor.byp[NHEFS.2$hist.cor.byp %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$hist.cor.byp <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$hist.cor.byp)
NHEFS.3$hist.cor.byp[NHEFS.3$hist.cor.byp %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   Unlike NHEFS data sets, NHANES.1 data set had two variables for medication of diabetes, one oral medication and one is insulin. We create a \texttt{med.dia} column for NHANES 1 by merging those two columns.

    For the other datasets, we clean the unnecessary information.

```{r}
NHANES.1$med.dia.ins <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$med.dia.ins)
NHANES.1$med.dia.oral <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$med.dia.oral)
NHANES.1 <- NHANES.1 |> 
  mutate(across(c(med.dia.ins, med.dia.oral), ~ na_if(., 8))) |>
  mutate(med.dia = case_when(
    med.dia.ins == 1 | med.dia.oral == 1         ~ 1,  
    med.dia.ins == 2 & med.dia.oral == 2         ~ 2,  
      TRUE                                       ~ NA_real_
    )) |> 
  select(-c("med.dia.oral", "med.dia.ins"))

NHEFS.1$med.dia <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$med.dia)
NHEFS.1$med.dia[NHEFS.1$med.dia %in% c(7, 8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$med.dia <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$med.dia)
NHEFS.2$med.dia[NHEFS.2$med.dia %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9, 96)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$med.dia <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$med.dia)
NHEFS.3$med.dia[NHEFS.3$med.dia %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9, 96)] <- NA

```

-   For the medication regarding high blood pressure, we do the same cleaning stuff for the NHEFS data sets.

    For the NHANES, there is an extra category: 3 which refers to \textit{no longer has high blood pressure}. We assign this category to the category presenting not taking medication.

```{r}
NHANES.1$med.hbp <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$med.hbp)
NHANES.1$med.hbp[NHANES.1$med.hbp %in% 3] <- 2

NHEFS.1$med.hbp <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$med.hbp)
NHEFS.1$med.hbp[NHEFS.1$med.hbp %in% c(7, 8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$med.hbp <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$med.hbp)
NHEFS.2$med.hbp[NHEFS.2$med.hbp %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9, 96)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$med.hbp <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$med.hbp)
NHEFS.3$med.hbp[NHEFS.3$med.hbp %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9, 96)] <- NA

```

-   We had age and height only for NHANES data set. We can add them Adding age and height on each data sets from the NHEFS data. The \texttt{height} variable (in inch) was in the format of 3 digit with the actual weight being XX.X inch. We mutated the column. Further, we roughly add 10, 12, 13 years to the age of a people in NHANES to get the age at three NHEFS data sets, respectively.

```{r}
NHANES.1$age <- as.numeric((NHANES.1$age))
NHANES.1$height <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$height)/10

key_demo <- NHANES.1 |>
  select(ssn, base_age = age, height)

NHEFS.1 <- NHEFS.1 |> left_join(key_demo, by = "ssn")
NHEFS.2 <- NHEFS.2 |> left_join(key_demo, by = "ssn")
NHEFS.3 <- NHEFS.3 |> left_join(key_demo, by = "ssn")

NHEFS.1 <- NHEFS.1 |> 
  mutate(age = base_age + 10) |> select(-base_age)                 

NHEFS.2 <- NHEFS.2 |> 
  mutate(age = base_age + 12) |> select(-base_age)

NHEFS.3 <- NHEFS.3 |> 
  mutate(age = base_age + 13) |> select(-base_age)

```

-   In the NHANES.1, the \texttt{weight} variable (in pounds) was in the format of 5 digit with the actual weight being XXX.XX. We mutated the column. For the NHEFS, we had some other entries corresponding to \textit{didn't respond}, \textit{incapable}, etc. We filled them by \texttt{NA}.

```{r}
NHANES.1$weight <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$weight)/100

NHEFS.1$weight <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$weight)
NHEFS.1$weight[NHEFS.1$weight %in% c(997, 995, 996, 999)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$weight <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$weight)
NHEFS.2$weight[NHEFS.2$weight %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$weight <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$weight)
NHEFS.3$weight[NHEFS.3$weight %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   Same goes for the \texttt{smoke} variable where there were uninformative entries which we replaced by \texttt{NA}.

```{r}
NHANES.1$smoke <- as.numeric(NHANES.1$smoke)

NHEFS.1$smoke <- as.numeric(NHEFS.1$smoke)
NHEFS.1$smoke[NHEFS.1$smoke %in% c(7, 8, 9)] <- NA

NHEFS.2$smoke <- as.numeric(NHEFS.2$smoke)
NHEFS.2$smoke[NHEFS.2$smoke %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

NHEFS.3$smoke <- as.numeric(NHEFS.3$smoke)
NHEFS.3$smoke[NHEFS.3$smoke %in% c(-1, -7, -8, -9)] <- NA

```

-   Alcohol history was a bit complicated. First we cleaned the unnecessary information. For the NHANES.1 data the categories are 1 for everyday, 2 for just about everyday, 3 for about 2 or 3 times a week, 4 for about 1-4 times a month, 5 for more than 3 but less than 12 times a year, and 6 for no more than 3 times a year. For the NHEFS.1 data they are 01-31 for number of days in a month, 94 for recently quit drinking, 95 for more than 3 but less than 12 times a year, and 96 for no more than 3 times a year. For NHEFS.2, they are 1-7 for number of days in a week, 94 for more than 3 but less than 12 times a year, and 95 for no more than 3 times a year. For NHEFS.3, they are 1-30 for number of days in a month, 94 for more than 3 but less than 12 times a year, 95 for no more than 3 times a year, and 0 for none. We bring all of them to a common scale with three categories: 1 for frequently, 2 for sometimes, and 3 for never or less than 3 times a year.

```{r}

NHANES.1 <- NHANES.1 |>
  mutate(alcohol = as.numeric(alcohol),
         alcohol = case_when(alcohol == 8               ~ NA_real_,      
                             alcohol %in% c(1, 2)       ~ 1,             
                             alcohol %in% c(3, 4, 5)    ~ 2,             
                             alcohol == 6               ~ 3,             
                             TRUE                       ~ NA_real_))

NHEFS.1 <- NHEFS.1 |>
  mutate(alcohol = as.numeric(alcohol),
         alcohol = case_when(alcohol %in% c(97, 98, 99)        ~ NA_real_,      
                             alcohol > 10 & alcohol < 32       ~ 1,             
                             alcohol < 11 | alcohol == 95      ~ 2,             
                             alcohol %in% c(94, 96)            ~ 3,           
                             TRUE                              ~ NA_real_))

NHEFS.2 <- NHEFS.2 |>
  mutate(alcohol = as.numeric(alcohol),
         alcohol = case_when(alcohol %in% c(97, 98, 99)        ~ NA_real_,      
                             alcohol > 2  & alcohol < 8        ~ 1,             
                             alcohol < 3  | alcohol == 94      ~ 2,             
                             alcohol == 95                     ~ 3,             
                             TRUE                              ~ NA_real_))

NHEFS.3 <- NHEFS.3 |>
  mutate(alcohol = as.numeric(alcohol),
         alcohol = case_when(alcohol %in% c(97, 98, 99)        ~ NA_real_,      
                             alcohol %in% c(0, 95)             ~ 3,             
                             alcohol > 10 & alcohol < 31       ~ 1,             
                             alcohol < 11 | alcohol == 94      ~ 2,             
                             TRUE                              ~ NA_real_))


```

## Description of the data

Based on the data preparation above, we describe the variables with the corresponding categories as below.

```{=tex}
\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Variables and their descriptions}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.2\linewidth}p{0.7\linewidth}}
\hline
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Description} \\ \hline
ssn          & Participant identifier \\ 
age          & Age (years) at the given wave \\ 
sex          & Sex (1: male, 2: female) \\ 
race         & Race (1: white, 2: black, 3: Others) \\ 
mar.st       & Marital status (1: married, 2: widowed, 3: divorced, 4: separated, 5: never married, and 6: Under 17) \\ 
vital.st     & Vital status at follow-up (1: alive, 3: dead) \\ 
gen.hlth     & Self-reported general health status (1: excellent, 2: very good, 3: good, 4: fair, and 5: poor) \\ 
height       & Baseline height (inches) \\ 
weight       & Weight at given wave (pounds) \\ 
smoke        & Current smoking status (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
alcohol      & Alcohol use status (1: Frequently, 2: Sometimes, 3: Almost Never) \\ 
hist.arth    & History of arthritis (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
hist.hrt.att & History of heart attack (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
hist.TIA     & History of transient ischemic attack (TIA) (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
hist.CVA     & History of cerebrovascular accident (stroke) (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
hist.cor.byp & History of coronary bypass surgery (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
med.hbp      & Takes medication for high blood pressure (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
med.dia      & Takes medication for diabetes (1: Yes, 2: No) \\ 
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

# EDA

We provide a handful of plots exploratory data analysis. Almost in all the plots we present instances of each wave for easy comparison.

\textbf{1. Age distribution by wave}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=2.15, fig.width=6}
bind_rows(NHANES.1, NHEFS.1, NHEFS.2, NHEFS.3) |>
filter(!is.na(age)) |> 
  select(age, wave) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = wave)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) + 
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Density", fill = "Wave") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5))

```

The age distributions shift markedly across waves: NHANES.1 includes many younger participants, while NHEFS.1–3 are increasingly dominated by older adults, with NHEFS.3 concentrated in the 60–80 range. This reflects natural aging and selective loss to follow-up or death, so any longitudinal comparisons or clustering across waves must account for this strong change in age structure and potential survivorship bias.

\textbf{2. Baseline age distribution of poeple who were eventually dead}

```{r echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6}
# indicator if ever dead by NHEFS.3
dead_ssn <- NHEFS.3$vital.st == 3
# assuming 3 = dead; adapt code as needed

NHANES.1 |>
  mutate(dead_any = ssn %in% NHEFS.3$ssn[dead_ssn]) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = dead_any)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Baseline age", y = "Density",
       fill = "Ever dead by wave 3",
       title = "") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5))

```

The baseline age distributions differ sharply by eventual vital status: those who died by wave 3 are overwhelmingly older at baseline, with density concentrated around the 60–70 age range, whereas survivors are much younger on average and have substantial mass in childhood and early adulthood. This highlights strong age‐related mortality and underscores the importance of adjusting for baseline age when interpreting longitudinal and clustering results.

\textbf{3. Distribution of height of the participants}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=2, fig.width=4}

NHANES.1 |> 
  mutate(height = as.numeric(height)) |> 
  select(height) |> drop_na() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = height)) + geom_density(col = "darkcyan") +
  labs(x = "Height of the NHANES cohort", y = "Density",
       title = "") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 9),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 11))
```

The above shows the kernel density of height for the NHANES cohort. We see that there are a lot of participants with shorter height indicating the prevalence of children. The height distributions for all survey waves are practically identical, so their density curves overlap and appear as a single curve in the plot.

\textbf{4. Weight distribution by wave}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=2.5, fig.width=6}
df.weight <- bind_rows(NHANES.1, NHEFS.1, NHEFS.2, NHEFS.3) |>
filter(!is.na(weight)) |> 
  select(weight, wave, ssn)

ggplot(df.weight, aes(x = weight, fill = wave)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) + 
  labs(title = "",
       x = "Weight (Pound)", y = "Density", fill = "Wave") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5))

```

The weight distributions show that NHANES.1 contains a lighter subgroup (children/adolescents) that disappears in the follow-up waves, which are concentrated in the adult range around 130–200 pounds. Across NHEFS.1–3 the main peak remains similar, suggesting only modest shifts in average weight over time relative to the strong compositional change from including vs. excluding younger participants.

\textbf{5. Weight trajectories for a random sample of 100 people}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=2.5, fig.width=5}

samp <- sample(which(unname(table(df.weight$ssn)) == 4), 100)
samp.ssn <- df.weight$ssn[samp]

df.weight |>
  filter(ssn %in% samp.ssn) |>
  mutate(wave = factor(wave)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = wave, y = weight, group = ssn, colour = ssn)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = "Wave", y = "Weight",
    title = ""
  ) +
  ylim(min(df.weight$weight), max(df.weight$weight)) +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5))


```

For this random sample of 100 participants, individual weight trajectories appear largely stable across waves: most lines fluctuate only modestly around their baseline values, with no systematic upward or downward trend. A few individuals show larger gains or losses, but there is no evidence of widespread drastic weight change in the cohort over time.

The left panel shows that most participants have no baseline conditions, with steadily fewer individuals as comorbidity count increases. df.nhf.2 <- data.frame(col = colnames(NHEFS.2),

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
df.miss <- list(df.nhf.1, df.nhf.2, df.nhf.3, df.nhn.1) |>
  reduce(full_join, by = "col") |>
  filter(!col %in% c("wave", "ssn"))

kable(df.miss, 
      caption = "Missingness of variabels at each wave\\label{tab:missing}")
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
  pivot_longer(cols = -Variable, names_to = "Wave", values_to = "prop_missing")

ggplot(df_long, aes(x = Wave, y = Variable, fill = prop_missing)) +

```

## Missing data patterns and implications

Table \ref{tab:missing} shows substantial heterogeneity in the amount of missing data across variables and waves. Identifiers and basic demographics such as \texttt{ssn}, \texttt{sex}, \texttt{race}, and \texttt{mar.st} are essentially complete in the NHEFS waves (missingness close to $0\%$), with only modest missingness at baseline for \texttt{race} and \texttt{mar.st} (about $13\%$). In contrast, several clinical and behavioural variables exhibit very high levels of missingness. For example, medication indicators \texttt{med.hbp} and \texttt{med.dia} are missing for roughly $70$--$80\%$ of subjects in the NHEFS waves and for nearly all subjects at baseline; the coronary bypass indicator \texttt{hist.cor.byp} is missing for about $80\%$ of subjects in NHEFS.2 and essentially $100\%$ in the other waves. Smoking and alcohol variables also suffer from considerable missingness: \texttt{smoke} is missing for roughly $60\%$ of participants in NHEFS.1 and almost all participants in NHEFS.2 and NHEFS.3, and \texttt{alcohol} is missing for about $40$--$60\%$ of subjects at most waves. Measures like \texttt{weight}, \texttt{height}, and derived \texttt{age} have moderate missingness (roughly $15$--$50\%$, depending on wave), while several history variables (\texttt{hist.hrt.att}, \texttt{hist.TIA}, \texttt{hist.CVA}, \texttt{hist.arth}) show a mixture of moderate ($15$--$40\%$) and extreme ($>90\%$) missingness across waves. General health (\texttt{gen.hlth}) is observed for only about half of the subjects in the NHEFS waves and not collected at all at baseline.

These patterns indicate that missingness is driven by a combination of study design (e.g., detailed examinations or questions asked only in subsamples or at particular waves) and subject characteristics, rather than being Missing Completely At Random (MCAR). In particular, the very high and correlated missingness for baseline clinical and behavioural variables such as \texttt{med.hbp}, \texttt{med.dia}, \texttt{smoke}, \texttt{alcohol}, and disease history measures suggests that baseline \emph{exam status} and underlying health are predictive of whether related data are observed in the NHEFS waves. Conversely, basic demographic variables (\texttt{sex}, \texttt{race}, \texttt{mar.st}) and identifiers (\texttt{ssn}) are essentially complete and therefore unlikely to drive missingness patterns.

\medskip\noindent \textbf{Implications for subsequent analysis.}

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Because missingness is strongly related to baseline health and to which questionnaire/exam modules were administered, complete–case analyses would disproportionately retain a healthier and more thoroughly examined subset of participants.  This would bias estimates of risk factor distributions and could distort any clustering of trajectories by under–representing high–risk or less compliant individuals.
  \item Several variables (notably \texttt{med.dia}, \texttt{med.hbp}, \texttt{hist.cor.byp}, and smoking history in later waves) are so sparsely observed that they are effectively unusable for longitudinal clustering unless one adopts a model that explicitly accounts for the missingness mechanism.  In practice, these variables may need to be excluded from the clustering feature set or handled via multiple imputation or joint modelling.
  \item Moderate missingness in key continuous variables such as \texttt{weight}, \texttt{height}, and \texttt{age}, together with differential loss to follow–up and mortality (summarised by \texttt{vital.st}), implies a risk of survivorship bias: subjects with worse baseline health are more likely to drop out or die, so observed follow–up data over–represent healthier trajectories.  Any clustering of longitudinal profiles should therefore acknowledge that the observed data arise from a selected subset of the original cohort.
\end{itemize}
```
Overall, the updated missingness table reinforces that the data are unlikely to be MCAR. Baseline health and examination variables are closely tied to the availability of follow–up measurements, and subsequent clustering or trajectory analyses must handle missing data explicitly rather than relying on naive complete–case methods.

## Distribution of \textit{ssn} in each data sets.

The following code generates a matrix where the diagonal elements show how many participants are in that particular data set. And for any $(i,j)$-th non-diagonal element, it gives the number of participants from $i$-th data set that is present on the $j$-th data set.

```{r}
dfs <- list( NHANES.1 = NHANES.1, NHEFS.1  = NHEFS.1,
             NHEFS.2  = NHEFS.2, NHEFS.3  = NHEFS.3)

# Unique ssn sets for each data set
# ssn_list <- purrr::map(dfs, ~ base::unique(.x$ssn))
# save(ssn_list, file = "ssn_list.Rdata")
load("ssn_list.Rdata")

overlap_count <- function(i, j) {
  sum(ssn_list[[i]] %in% ssn_list[[j]])
}

n_sets <- length(ssn_list)
overlap_mat <- matrix(
  nrow = n_sets, ncol = n_sets,
  dimnames = list(names(ssn_list), names(ssn_list))
)

for (i in seq_len(n_sets)) {
  for (j in seq_len(n_sets)) {
    overlap_mat[i, j] <- overlap_count(i, j)
  }
}

overlap_mat
```

We see that the NHANES.1 data set is the super set and all the participants from the subsequent NHEFS waves are in NHANES.1. The same goes for NHEFS.1 data set. It contains all participants from following NHEFS data sets.

Things change for NHEFS.2 data set. We see that among 5677 participants only 2894 participants are in NHEFS.3 and there are (9998-2894) = `r 9998-2894` extra participant that are not in NHEFS.02. This is a common phenomena in longitudinal study which can be attributed to funding availability or participants willingness to take part again, or maybe mere designing.

In summary, we see the only `r min(overlap_mat)` participants are common in the four data sets, which is respectively `r min(overlap_mat)/nrow(NHANES.1)`, `r min(overlap_mat)/nrow(NHEFS.1)`, `r min(overlap_mat)/nrow(NHEFS.2)`, and `r min(overlap_mat)/nrow(NHEFS.3)` proportions of data for the NHANES, NHEFS 1, NHEFS 2, and NHEFS 3 data set.

Below we subset the NHEFS.03 data set to all the common participants who were also in NHEFS.02 data set to make things easier and easy to interpret.

```{r}
ssn_keep <- intersect(unique(NHEFS.2$ssn), unique(NHEFS.3$ssn))

NHEFS.3.com  <- NHEFS.3  |> filter(ssn %in% ssn_keep)

```

# Clustering NHANES data

We start with subsetting the NHANES data set. We choose complete case rows and also we choose variables which will keep the number of participants within a reasonable range.

```{r}

# Choosing variables for clustering the NHANES I data set

vars_cont <- c("age", "height", "weight")
vars_cat  <- c( "sex", "race", "mar.st", "gen.hlth", "alcohol",
                "hist.hrt.att", "hist.CVA", "hist.arth")

NHANES.1.sub <- NHANES.1 |>
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |>
  filter(complete.cases(across(-ssn))) |>
  mutate(across(any_of(vars_cat), as.factor))

dim(NHANES.1.sub)

```

We see that there are altogether `r nrow(NHANES.1.sub)` participants with complete cases for the variables chosen above. We fit the four methods one by one on this subset of NHANES data set.

\textbf{There could have been a better way of handling the missing data but we couldn't explore due to the lack of time.}

## Fiting the k-means clusering

```{r fig.align='center', fig.height=3, fig.width=5}

# selecting variables with only 1 level
one_level_vars <- NHANES.1.sub |>
  select(-ssn) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), n_distinct)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_levels") |>
  filter(n_levels <= 1) |>
  pull(variable)

nhanes_km <- NHANES.1.sub |>
  select(-all_of(one_level_vars))

# creating the design matrix and scaling
X_base <- model.matrix(~ . - ssn - 1, data = nhanes_km)
X_base_scaled <- scale(X_base)

# Running k-means for several K
K_grid <- 2:15

set.seed(50)
seeds <- sample.int(1e7, length(K_grid))

  ggplot(aes(x = K, y = WSS)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +

        axis.title = element_text(size = 12))
 
```

Even with the \texttt{set.seed()} option, we get different results for different run. But based on multiple run of the code, $K=6$ seems to be a good choice.

```{r}

# Choosing K and fit final k-means

K_choose <- 6

set.seed(2025)
km_final <- kmeans(X_base_scaled, centers = K_choose, nstart = 100)

NHANES.1.sub <- NHANES.1.sub |>
  mutate(cluster_km = factor(km_final$cluster))

# cluster sizes
table(NHANES.1.sub$cluster_km)
```

\newpage
## Fiting the Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model

To cluster the baseline NHANES I subjects we treat each participant $i=1,\dots,N$ as having a $D$–dimensional vector of standardized features $\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1},\dots,x_{iD})^\top$ constructed from age, height, weight, and selected categorical variables (after dummy coding and centering / scaling). We assume that the population is a finite mixture of $K$ latent subpopulations (clusters). Let $z_i \in \{1,\dots,K\}$ denote the latent cluster allocation for subject $i$, and let $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1,\dots,\theta_K)^\top$ be the corresponding vector of mixing proportions.

\paragraph{Latent allocation and observation model.}

Conditional on the mixture weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, the cluster indicator for subject $i$ follows a categorical distribution, $$  z_i \,\mid\, \boldsymbol{\theta} \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}(\boldsymbol{\theta}),
  \qquad i = 1,\dots,N.$$ Given $z_i = k$, the feature vector $\mathbf{x}_i$ is assumed to arise from a $D$–dimensional Gaussian distribution with cluster–specific mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k = (\mu_{k1},\dots,\mu_{kD})^\top$ and diagonal covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_k = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{k1}^2,\dots,\sigma_{kD}^2)$: $$\mathbf{x}_i \,\mid\, z_i = k,\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\sigma}_k
  \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}_D\!\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,
      \mathbf{\Sigma}_k \big),
  \qquad k = 1,\dots,K,$$ where $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_k = (\sigma_{k1},\dots,\sigma_{kD})^\top$ collects the cluster–specific standard deviations.

Marginalising over $z_i$ yields the usual finite mixture representation, $$  p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, \{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_k\}_{k=1}^K)
  \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^K \theta_k \,
        \mathcal{N}_D\!\big(\mathbf{x}_i \mid
        \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \mathbf{\Sigma}_k \big).$$

\paragraph{Prior distributions.}

We place weakly informative priors on the mixing weights, cluster means, and cluster–specific standard deviations. In particular, $$  \boldsymbol{\theta} \;\sim\; \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K),
  \qquad\text{with } \alpha_k = 1 \text{ for all } k,$$ so that a priori all cluster sizes are equally likely. For the Gaussian parameters we use independent priors across clusters and dimensions, $$  \mu_{kd} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2),
  \qquad
  \sigma_{kd} \;\sim\; \text{Lognormal}(0, \sigma_\ell^2),
  \qquad k = 1,\dots,K,\; d = 1,\dots,D,$$ with $\tau^2$ and $\sigma_\ell^2$ chosen to be moderately large (in our implementation we take $\tau = 2$ and $\sigma_\ell = 0.5$) so that the priors are weakly informative on the standardized scale.

We encode the above model in the following Stan code.

```{r}

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

bgmm_stan_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;              // number of subjects
  int<lower=1> D;              // number of features
  int<lower=1> K;              // number of clusters
  matrix[N, D] X;              // scaled features
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;            // mixing proportions
  matrix[K, D] mu;             // cluster means
  matrix<lower=0>[K, D] sigma; // cluster-specific SDs (diagonal covariances)
}
model {
  // priors
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0, K));          // vague Dirichlet
  to_vector(mu)    ~ normal(0, 2);                // weakly informative
  to_vector(sigma) ~ lognormal(0, 0.5);           // positive SDs

  // likelihood (marginal over latent labels)
  for (n in 1:N) {
    vector[K] lps;
    for (k in 1:K) {
      lps[k] = log(theta[k]);
      for (d in 1:D) {
        lps[k] += normal_lpdf(X[n, d] | mu[k, d], sigma[k, d]);
      }
    }
    target += log_sum_exp(lps);
  }
}
"
```

We fit the model with the same scaled data matrix we created while fitting the k-means clustering.

```{r}

N <- nrow(X_base_scaled)
D <- ncol(X_base_scaled)
K <- K_choose

bgmm_data <- list(N = N, D = D, K = K, X = X_base_scaled)
```

Now we obtain the cluster assignments with the following code.

```{r}

# computing posterior means for theta, mu, sigma
theta_hat <- bgmm_list.0[[1]]
mu_hat    <- bgmm_list.0[[2]]   
sigma_hat <- bgmm_list.0[[3]]

# computing posterior cluster probabilities for each individual
log_resp <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = N, ncol = K)

for (n in 1:N) {
  for (k in 1:K) {
    lp <- log(theta_hat[k])
    for (d in 1:D) {
      lp <- lp + dnorm(X_base_scaled[n, d],
                       mean = mu_hat[k, d],
                       sd   = sigma_hat[k, d],
                       log  = TRUE)
    }
    log_resp[n, k] <- lp
  }
}

# normalizing to probabilities
resp <- exp(log_resp - apply(log_resp, 1, max))
resp <- resp / rowSums(resp)

# MAP cluster labels
cluster_bgmm <- max.col(resp)     

NHANES.1.sub$cluster_bgmm <- factor(cluster_bgmm)

# cluster sizes
table(NHANES.1.sub$cluster_bgmm)
```

## Fiting the CLAMR Model

To incorporate clinical knowledge about plausible ranges of baseline variables,
we also fit the CLAMR (Clinically informed Latent Allocation Mixture Regression)
model in the spirit of @dombowsky2025bayesian to the baseline NHANES I data.  As
before, each subject $i=1,\dots,N$ has a $D$–dimensional feature vector
$\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1},\dots,x_{iD})^\top$, but here we restrict attention to
continuous baseline variables such as age, height, and weight for which it is
meaningful to define clinically interpretable ranges.

We assume a finite mixture of $K$ latent clusters with mixing proportions
$\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1,\dots,\theta_K)^\top$ and cluster–specific
means $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k = (\mu_{k1},\dots,\mu_{kD})^\top$ and diagonal
covariance matrices
$\mathbf{\Sigma}_k = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{k1}^2,\dots,\sigma_{kD}^2)$.

\paragraph{Meaningful regions for each feature.}
For each continuous feature $d \in \{1,\dots,D\}$ we define
$L$ \emph{meaningful regions} (MRs) on the real line,
$$\mathcal{R}_{d1}, \dots, \mathcal{R}_{dL} \subset \mathbb{R},$$
intended to correspond to clinically interpretable ranges such as ``low'',
``normal'', and ``high'' values.  In our implementation we take $L = 3$ and
construct these regions from the empirical tertiles of the baseline
distribution of $x_{\cdot d}$:
$$  \mathcal{R}_{d1} = [q_{d,0}, q_{d,1/3}], \quad
  \mathcal{R}_{d2} = (q_{d,1/3}, q_{d,2/3}], \quad
  \mathcal{R}_{d3} = (q_{d,2/3}, q_{d,1}],$$
where $q_{d,p}$ denotes the $p$th empirical quantile of $x_{\cdot d}$ and
$q_{d,0}, q_{d,1}$ are the minimum and maximum.  For each region
$\mathcal{R}_{d\ell} = [a_{d\ell}, b_{d\ell}]$ we define a midpoint
$m_{d\ell} = (a_{d\ell} + b_{d\ell})/2$ and a kernel standard deviation
$\tau_{d\ell}$ chosen so that a Normal distribution with mean $m_{d\ell}$ and
standard deviation $\tau_{d\ell}$ places most of its mass inside the interval;
in practice we take
$$\tau_{d\ell} \approx \frac{b_{d\ell} - a_{d\ell}}{2 z_{0.975}},$$
so that roughly $95\%$ of the mass lies in $[a_{d\ell}, b_{d\ell}]$.

\paragraph{Latent allocation and likelihood.}
Conditional on the mixing proportions $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, the cluster
indicator for subject $i$ is
$$  z_i \,\mid\, \boldsymbol{\theta} \;\sim\;
  \mathrm{Categorical}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), \qquad i = 1,\dots,N.$$
Given $z_i = k$ and the cluster–specific parameters, the continuous feature
vector obeys a diagonal–covariance Gaussian model
$$  \mathbf{x}_i \,\mid\, z_i = k,\,
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\sigma}_k
  \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}_D\!\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,
      \mathbf{\Sigma}_k\big),$$
where $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_k = (\sigma_{k1},\dots,\sigma_{kD})^\top$ and
$\mathbf{\Sigma}_k = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{k1}^2,\dots,\sigma_{kD}^2)$.
Marginalising over $z_i$ again yields the finite mixture density
$$  p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\theta},
      \{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_k\}_{k=1}^K)
  \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^K \theta_k \,
        \mathcal{N}_D\!\big(\mathbf{x}_i \mid
        \boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\mathbf{\Sigma}_k\big).$$

\paragraph{CLAMR prior on cluster centers.}
The key difference between CLAMR and the standard Gaussian mixture model lies
in the prior for the cluster centers $\mu_{kd}$.  For each feature $d$ we
introduce a simplex
$\boldsymbol{\pi}_d = (\pi_{d1},\dots,\pi_{dL})^\top$ of probabilities over
its meaningful regions.  We assign a Dirichlet prior,
$$  \boldsymbol{\pi}_d \;\sim\;
  \mathrm{Dirichlet}(\alpha_{d1},\dots,\alpha_{dL}),
  \qquad d = 1,\dots,D,$$
with $\alpha_{d\ell} = 1$ in our implementation to represent a priori
indifference among regions.

Conditional on $\boldsymbol{\pi}_d$, the prior for each cluster center
coordinate $\mu_{kd}$ is a mixture of Gaussian kernels centred at the MR
midpoints,
$$  p(\mu_{kd} \mid \boldsymbol{\pi}_d)
  \;=\; \sum_{\ell=1}^L \pi_{d\ell}
        \,\mathcal{N}\!\big(\mu_{kd} \mid m_{d\ell}, \tau_{d\ell}^2\big),
  \qquad k = 1,\dots,K, \; d = 1,\dots,D.$$
This construction encourages each cluster mean to lie near one of the
clinically meaningful regions for that feature, while still allowing the data
to update both the location and the relative weight of the regions through
$\boldsymbol{\pi}_d$.

For the remaining parameters we use weakly informative priors similar to the
standard Bayesian Gaussian mixture:
$$  \boldsymbol{\theta} \;\sim\; \mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1), \qquad
  \sigma_{kd} \;\sim\; \mathrm{Lognormal}(0, 0.5^2),
  \quad k = 1,\dots,K,\; d = 1,\dots,D.$$
  
We encode the above model in the following Stan code.

```{r}

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

clamr_stan_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;              // subjects
  int<lower=1> D;              // features
  int<lower=1> K;              // overfitted # of clusters
  int<lower=1> L;              // # meaningful regions per feature

  matrix[N, D] X;              // data (original scale)

  // CLAMR prior hyperparameters:
  matrix[D, L] mr_mid;         // midpoints of MRs for each feature
  matrix[D, L] mr_sd;          // SDs for each MR kernel
  matrix[D, L] alpha_mr;       // Dirichlet params for MR probs 
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;            // mixing proportions

  matrix[K, D] mu;             // cluster centers
  matrix<lower=0>[K, D] sigma; // cluster SDs (diagonal covariance)

  // MR probabilities per feature (each row is a simplex over L regions)
  simplex[L] pi_mr[D];
}
model {
  // Priors on mixture weights and variances
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0, K));
  to_vector(sigma) ~ lognormal(0, 0.5);

  // Prior on MR probabilities for each feature
  for (d in 1:D) {
    pi_mr[d] ~ dirichlet( to_vector(alpha_mr[d]) );
  }

  // CLAMR prior on cluster centers: mixture of Gaussian kernels over MRs
  for (k in 1:K) {
    for (d in 1:D) {
      vector[L] lp_comp;
      for (l in 1:L) {
        lp_comp[l] = log(pi_mr[d][l]) +
                     normal_lpdf(mu[k, d] | mr_mid[d, l], mr_sd[d, l]);
      }
      target += log_sum_exp(lp_comp);
    }
  }

  // Likelihood: diagonal Gaussian mixture
  for (n in 1:N) {
    vector[K] lp_cluster;
    for (k in 1:K) {
      lp_cluster[k] = log(theta[k]);
      for (d in 1:D) {
        lp_cluster[k] += normal_lpdf(X[n, d] | mu[k, d], sigma[k, d]);
      }
    }
    target += log_sum_exp(lp_cluster);
  }
}
"

```

Now we prepare the dataset required for fitting the model. We take the continuous variables and define meaningful regions for each of them. We take $L=3$ for each of the continuous variable, denoting high, normal and low regions.

```{r}

mr_vars <- vars_cont

# subset to the continuous variables
nhanes_clamr <- NHANES.1.sub |>
  select(ssn, all_of(mr_vars))

L <- 3

# computing MR boundaries using empirical tertiles
mr_bounds <- lapply(mr_vars, function(v) {
  x <- nhanes_clamr[[v]]
  qs <- quantile(x, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
  as.numeric(qs)
})
names(mr_bounds) <- mr_vars

# midpoints and within-region SDs for CLAMR prior
# we choose sigma so that about 95% of a Normal lies inside each interval
z975 <- qnorm(0.975)

mr_mid <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(mr_vars), ncol = L)
mr_sd  <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(mr_vars), ncol = L)

for (j in seq_along(mr_vars)) {
  b <- mr_bounds[[j]]
  for (l in 1:L) {
    a_l <- b[l]
    b_l <- b[l + 1]
    mr_mid[j, l] <- (a_l + b_l) / 2
    mr_sd[j, l]  <- (b_l - a_l) / (2 * z975)  # so ~95% lies in [a_l, b_l]
  }
}

# simpling symmetric Dirichlet hyperparameters over MRs 
alpha_mr <- matrix(1, nrow = length(mr_vars), ncol = L)

# building the data matrix for modeling 
X_clamr <- as.matrix(nhanes_clamr[, mr_vars])

N <- nrow(X_clamr)
D <- ncol(X_clamr)
K <- K_choose

clamr_data <- list(
  N       = N,
  D       = D,
  K       = K,
  L       = L,
  X       = X_clamr,
  mr_mid  = mr_mid,
  mr_sd   = mr_sd,
  alpha_mr = alpha_mr
)

```

## Fitting the Bayesian pyramid method

To flexibly model the joint distribution of multivariate categorical baseline
variables, we also consider the Bayesian Pyramids framework of @gu2023bayesian,
which introduces a multilayer discrete latent structure specifically tailored to
high-dimensional unordered categorical data.  Let
$$\mathbf{y}_i = (y_{i1},\dots,y_{ip})^\top, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n,$$
denote the $p$ observed categorical variables for subject $i$, with
$y_{ij} \in \{1,\dots,d_j\}$ and $d_j$ the number of categories for variable
$j$.

\paragraph{Multilayer latent structure.}
Bayesian Pyramids posit several layers of binary latent variables arranged in a
``pyramid'' shape.  Let $D$ denote the number of latent layers (the depth of
the pyramid).  The layer closest to the observed data is
$$  \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)} =
  \big(\alpha_{i1}^{(1)},\dots,\alpha_{iK_1}^{(1)}\big)^\top
  \in \{0,1\}^{K_1},$$
and for $m = 1,\dots,D-1$ we introduce deeper layers
$$\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m+1)} \in \{0,1\}^{K_{m+1}},$$
with $K_{m+1} \le K_m$ so that the number of latent variables decreases as we
move deeper in the pyramid.  At the very top of the hierarchy, there is a
single discrete latent variable
$$z_i = z_i^{(D)} \in \{1,\dots,B\},$$
which can be interpreted as a coarse high-level cluster or latent class.  The
complete latent architecture therefore consists of $D$ latent layers plus the
observed layer at the bottom.

\paragraph{Pyramid-shaped Bayesian network and factorization.}
The latent and observed variables are linked via a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
with edges only between adjacent layers and directed from deep to shallow
(top--down).  There are no edges within a layer.  Writing
$\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m)} = (\alpha_{i1}^{(m)},\dots,\alpha_{iK_m}^{(m)})$
for layer $m$ and suppressing the dependence on $i$ for notational simplicity,
the joint distribution of $\mathbf{y}_i$, the latent layers
$\{\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m)}\}_{m=1}^{D-1}$, and the top latent $z_i$ admits
the factorization
\begin{align}
  P\!\big(\mathbf{y}_i, \{\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m)}\}_{m=1}^{D-1}, z_i\big)
  &= P\!\big(\mathbf{y}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)}\big)
     \prod_{m=1}^{D-2}
       P\!\big(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m)} \mid
               \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m+1)}\big)
       \,P\!\big(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(D-1)} \mid z_i\big)\,
       P(z_i).
  \label{eq:bpyramid_factor}
\end{align}
The conditional distribution of $\mathbf{y}_i$ given the closest latent layer
$\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)}$ factorizes across coordinates,
$$  P\!\big(\mathbf{y}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)}\big)
  = \prod_{j=1}^p P\!\big(y_{ij} \mid
      \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)}\big),$$
with each $P(y_{ij} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)})$ modelled using a
multinomial logistic regression on a subset of the binary latent features
in $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)}$.  Analogously, each deeper layer
$\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m)}$ is modelled conditionally on the next deeper
layer $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(m+1)}$---again via logistic regressions---with
sparse parent sets encoded by binary graphical matrices.  This pyramid-shaped
Bayesian network induces rich dependence among the observed variables while
maintaining parsimony and interpretability.

\paragraph{Two-latent-layer Bayesian Pyramid and inference.}
For applied work the authors focus on a two-latent-layer model, which we also
adopt in our implementation.  In this case, each subject has:
\begin{itemize}
  \item a top latent class $z_i \in \{1,\dots,B\}$, representing a coarse
        discrete cluster; and
  \item a vector of binary latent features
        $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)} \in \{0,1\}^{K_1}$, representing more
        granular latent traits.
\end{itemize}
The conditional distributions
$P(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)} \mid z_i)$ and
$P(y_{ij} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i^{(1)})$ are specified via logistic and
multinomial-logit regressions with sparse connectivity, and a shrinkage prior
is placed on the regression coefficients and graphical connections to favour
parsimonious latent structure.  Posterior computation proceeds via a tailored
Gibbs sampler using Pólya–Gamma data augmentation for the logistic components,
which allows efficient updating of both the latent binary vectors and the
regression parameters.

We encode the above model in the following Stan code.

```{r}

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

pyramid_stan_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;                     // number of subjects
  int<lower=1> P;                     // number of variables
  int<lower=1> K;                     // number of clusters
  int<lower=1> C[P];                  // number of categories per variable
  int<lower=1> Y[N, P];               // categorical responses (1..C[p])
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;                   // mixing proportions
  // phi[k, p] is a simplex over categories 1..C[p]
  simplex[C[p]] phi[K, P];            // cluster- and variable-specific probs
}
model {
  // priors
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0, K));      // vague over cluster sizes
  for (k in 1:K) {
    for (p in 1:P) {
      phi[k, p] ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0, C[p])); // uniform over categories
    }
  }

  // likelihood, marginalizing over z_i
  for (n in 1:N) {
    vector[K] lp_k;
    for (k in 1:K) {
      lp_k[k] = log(theta[k]);
      for (p in 1:P) {
        lp_k[k] += categorical_lpmf(Y[n, p] | phi[k, p]);
      }
    }
    target += log_sum_exp(lp_k);
  }
}
"
```

Similar as before, we now prepare the datasets.

```{r}

vars_pyr <- vars_cat

nhanes_pyr <- NHANES.1.sub |> select(ssn, any_of(vars_pyr)) |> 
  mutate(across(all_of(vars_pyr), ~ as.integer(factor(.))))

# integer matrix of categories

N <- nrow(Y_cat)
P <- ncol(Y_cat)

# number of categories per variable j

C_max <- max(C)
K_pyr <- K_choose

pyr_data <- list(
  N     = N,
  P     = P,
  K     = K_pyr,
  C_max = C_max,
  Y     = Y_cat
)

```

We fit the model as follows.

```{r}
phi_hat <- pyr_list.0[[2]]

# computing log posterior responsibilities given a
#           log p(z_i = k | Y_i, theta_hat, phi_hat)
```

## Finding similarities between clustering procedures

We calculate the similarities between the clusters by calculating the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) using the \texttt{adjustedRandIndex()} function from the \texttt{hclust} package.

```{r}

df_clust <- NHANES.1.sub

# Calculating ARIs
(ari_km_bgmm    <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_km,
                                     df_clust$cluster_bgmm))
(ari_km_clamr   <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_km,
                                     df_clust$cluster_clamr))
(ari_km_pyr     <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_km,
                                     df_clust$cluster_pyr))
(ari_bgmm_clamr <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_bgmm,
                                     df_clust$cluster_clamr))
(ari_bgmm_pyr   <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_bgmm,
                                     df_clust$cluster_pyr))
(ari_clamr_pyr  <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_clamr, 
                                     df_clust$cluster_pyr))

```

We see that the results are \textbf{not at all good}.

\newpage

## Implementation and practical challenges

For $K$–means we first dummy–coded categorical variables and standardized all features to have a mean of zero and unit variance.  Because the algorithm cannot handle missing values, we restricted attention to subjects with complete data on the selected baseline covariates, resulting in $n = $ `r nrow(nhanes_km)` individuals.  The number of clusters was chosen as $K = 6$ based on an elbow plot of the within–cluster sum of squares and interpretability of the resulting clusters.

The BGMM used the same standardized design matrix and assumed a finite mixture of $K$ multivariate Gaussians with diagonal covariance matrices and weakly informative priors on the mixture weights, means, and standard deviations.  Implementing the BGMM was computationally demanding with $n = $ `r nrow(nhanes_km)` complete cases, $D = $ `r ncol(X_base)` features, and $K = 6$ clusters, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo required several thousand iterations per chain to achieve good mixing. 

The CLAMR model retained the Gaussian mixture likelihood but replaced the Gaussian priors on cluster centres with mixture–of–Gaussians priors centred on clinically meaningful regions (MRs) for each continuous variable (e.g.\ tertile-based `low/normal/high' ranges for age, height, and weight).  A practical challenge was specifying these MRs in a principled way using NHANES~I, particularly in the absence of pre–defined clinical cutpoints, and the resulting Stan model was substantially more complex than the standard BGMM. Moreover, CLAMR is naturally defined only for continuous variables, so we applied it to a reduced set of continuous baseline covariates.

Finally, Bayesian Pyramids were implemented as a latent class model for multivariate categorical data, using a subset of baseline variables recoded as finite–valued categories (e.g.\ sex, age, race, marital status, general health).  The model assumes that, given a top–layer latent class $z_i \in \{1,\dots,K\}$, the observed categorical responses are conditionally independent multinomials with class–specific category probabilities.  Challenges here included deciding how aggressively to discretise continuous variables and handling the additional loss of sample size due to requiring complete cases on all selected categorical covariates.

\newpage

## Most influencial feature for determining the clustering

To identify which baseline features were most influential in determining cluster membership, we examined the extent to which each variable differed across clusters for each method.  For continuous variables we computed the $F$--statistic from one--way ANOVA of the form $x_j \sim \text{cluster}$, while for categorical variables we used the chi--square statistic from contingency tables between the variable and the cluster labels.  Variables with larger $F$ or chi--square statistics were interpreted as having a stronger association with cluster membership.


```{r}

# defining a function

cluster_var_importance <- function(df, cluster_var, cont_vars, cat_vars) {
  cl <- df[[cluster_var]]
  
  # continuous: ANOVA F-stat
  cont_res <- map_dfr(cont_vars, function(v) {
    x <- df[[v]]
    idx <- complete.cases(cl, x)
    if (length(unique(cl[idx])) < 2) return(NULL)
    fit <- lm(x[idx] ~ cl[idx])
    aov_tab <- anova(fit)
    tibble(
      variable = v,
      type     = "continuous",
      stat     = aov_tab$`F value`[1]
    )
  })
  
  # categorical: chi-square
  cat_res <- map_dfr(cat_vars, function(v) {
    x <- df[[v]]
    idx <- complete.cases(cl, x)
    tab <- table(cl[idx], x[idx])
    if (any(dim(tab) < 2)) return(NULL)
    chi <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
    tibble(
      variable = v,
      type     = "categorical",
      stat     = unname(chi$statistic)
    )
  })
  
  bind_rows(cont_res, cat_res) |>
    arrange(desc(stat))
}

df_inf.feat <- NHANES.1.sub
vars_cont <- c("age", "height", "weight")
vars_cat  <- c("sex", "race", "mar.st", "gen.hlth", "alcohol",
               "hist.hrt.att", "hist.CVA", "hist.arth")

imp_km    <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_km",    
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat) 
imp_bgmm  <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_bgmm",  
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat)
imp_clamr <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_clamr", 
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat)
imp_pyr   <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_pyr",   
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat)

(var_rank_tbl <- tibble(Rank  = 1:9, km = imp_km$variable,
                       bgmm  = imp_km$variable, clamr = imp_clamr$variable, 
                       pyr   = imp_pyr$variable))
```

The resulting rankings are broadly consistent across methods the above table.  In particular, \texttt{gen.hlth} is the top–ranked variable for k–means, BGMM, and the Bayesian Pyramids model, indicating that self–reported general health status is a primary driver of cluster separation.  Age and body size variables (especially weight and height) are also highly influential: CLAMR places age and weight in the top two positions, and these variables appear in the upper half of the rankings for all methods.

Among the remaining categorical covariates, race and marital status (\texttt{race}, \texttt{mar.st}) are consistently near the top of the rankings for k–means, BGMM, and Pyramids, while sex and alcohol use (\texttt{sex}, \texttt{alcohol}) occupy middle ranks, suggesting that they contribute to cluster structure but less strongly than general health and age/weight. History of arthritis (\texttt{hist.arth}) is particularly important for CLAMR and Pyramids, where it enters in the top six variables, reflecting that some clusters are characterised by a higher burden of musculoskeletal disease. Overall, the four methods agree that general health status, age, body size, race, marital status, and musculoskeletal/behavioural indicators are the key features defining the baseline clusters, with CLAMR emphasising age and weight more strongly and the Pyramids model placing relatively greater weight on discrete health and sociodemographic variables.

## Relationship between baseline clusters and subsequent mortality

```{r}

mort_df <- NHANES.1.sub |>
  select(ssn, cluster_km, cluster_bgmm, cluster_clamr, cluster_pyr) |>
  left_join( NHEFS.1 |> select(ssn, vital1 = vital.st), by = "ssn" ) |>
  left_join(NHEFS.2 |> select(ssn, vital2 = vital.st), by = "ssn") |>
  left_join(NHEFS.3 |> select(ssn, vital3 = vital.st), by = "ssn") |>
  mutate(
    dead = case_when(vital1 == 3 | vital2 == 3 | vital3 == 3 ~ 1L,   
                     TRUE                                    ~ 0L)) |> 
  select(!c("vital1", "vital2", "vital3"))

mort_by_km   <- mort_df |> group_by(cluster_km)  |> 
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(dead), risk = deaths/n)
mort_by_bgmm  <- mort_df |> group_by(cluster_bgmm)  |> 
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(dead), risk = deaths/n)
mort_by_clamr <- mort_df |> group_by(cluster_clamr) |> 
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(dead), risk = deaths/n)
mort_by_pyr   <- mort_df |> group_by(cluster_pyr)   |> 
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(dead), risk = deaths/n)

```

Let's focus on the CLAMR clustering. Below we plot two plots to show the relationship between mortality and clustering: one for the categorical variables and one for the continuous variables.

The top plot below shows the distribution of the continuous variables across all clusters and colored the cluster according to the mortality risk.

And the subsequent plot shows the distribution of the categorical variables across all clusters and the cluster level mortality risk is mentioned in the panel headings.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

df.plot <- mort_df |>
  left_join(NHANES.1.sub |> select(ssn, gen.hlth, race, mar.st, sex, age,
                                    height, weight), by = "ssn") |>
  mutate(weight = weight * 0.45359237) |>  
  left_join(mort_by_clamr |> select(cluster_clamr, risk), 
            by = "cluster_clamr") |>
  mutate(cluster_clamr = factor(cluster_clamr,
                           levels = sort(unique(cluster_clamr))))

df.plot.long <- df.plot |> pivot_longer( cols = c(age, height, weight),
                                          names_to  = "variable",
                                          values_to = "value") |> 
  mutate(cluster_clamr = paste0("Cluster: ", cluster_clamr))

ggplot(df.plot.long, aes(x = variable, y = value, fill = risk)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster_clamr, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_gradient(name  = "Mortality risk",
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    low   = "green", high  = "red") +
  labs( x = "CLAMR cluster variables", y = "Value",
    title = "Distribution of continuous variable by CLAMR cluster",
    subtitle = "Coloured by cluster mortality risk") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

cat_vars <- c("gen.hlth", "race", "mar.st", "sex")

df.cat <- mort_df |> left_join(NHANES.1.sub |> 
                      select(ssn, all_of(cat_vars)), by = "ssn") |>
  left_join(mort_by_clamr |> select(cluster_clamr, risk),
            by = "cluster_clamr") |>
  mutate(cluster_clamr = factor(cluster_clamr,
                        levels = sort(unique(cluster_clamr))))

df.cat.long <- df.cat |> pivot_longer(all_of(cat_vars),
                                       names_to = "variable",
                                       values_to = "level") |>
  filter(!is.na(level))

cat_props <- df.cat.long |>
  group_by(cluster_clamr, variable, level) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

lab_df <- mort_by_clamr |>
  mutate(
    cluster_clamr = factor(cluster_clamr,
                           levels = sort(unique(cluster_clamr))),
    lab = paste0("Cluster: ", cluster_clamr, ", Risk: ", percent(risk, 1))
  )
lab_vec <- setNames(lab_df$lab, lab_df$cluster_clamr)

ggplot(cat_props, aes(x = variable, y = prop, fill = level)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  facet_wrap( ~ cluster_clamr,
    labeller = labeller(cluster_clamr = lab_vec)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Baseline categorical variable",
       y = "Proportion within cluster", fill = "Category",
       title = "Distribution of categorical variable by CLAMR cluster",
       subtitle = "With mortality risk") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

The above two plots summarize the distribution of key baseline variables by CLAMR cluster, with mortality risk either encoded in the colour scale (continuous variables) or reported in the facet labels (categorical variables).  These plots show that \textit{certain clusters can clearly be characterised as higher risk than others}.  

In particular, cluster~5 has the highest mortality risk (approximately $52\%$) and is characterized by the oldest participants and comparatively high body weight.  Clusters~3 and~4 also display elevated mortality (roughly $17$--$21\%$) and contain individuals who are older and heavier than the overall sample, especially in cluster~3 where both height and weight are shifted upwards.  Cluster~1 has intermediate age and weight and a moderate mortality risk ($\approx 13\%$), whereas clusters~2 and~6, which consist of the youngest and lightest individuals, have the lowest mortality risks ($\approx 5\%$ and $2\%$, respectively).  Overall, the continuous plot reveals a monotone association: clusters representing older, heavier subjects correspond to higher mortality, while clusters of younger, lighter subjects are low risk.

The categorical plot provides additional context for these differences.  For each cluster, the within–cluster distributions of baseline general health, marital status, race, and sex are shown.  High–risk clusters, particularly cluster~5 and, to a lesser extent, clusters~3 and~4, have a larger share of individuals in the less favourable categories of general health and marital status (e.g.\ non-reference categories indicating poorer health or non-married states), whereas low–risk clusters~2 and~6 are dominated by the more favorable categories.  In contrast, the distributions of race and sex vary little across clusters, suggesting these variables play a smaller role in driving mortality differences than age, body size, and general health.  Taken together, the two figures show that the CLAMR clustering captures clinically meaningful strata of mortality risk: high–risk clusters (primarily clusters~5, 3, and~4) group older, heavier individuals with poorer self-reported health, while low–risk clusters (clusters~2 and~6) correspond to younger, healthier participants, with cluster~1 lying in between.

# Clustering the NHEFS data sets

For the NHEFS data set, we subset them to a common group of participants to make comparisons more interpretable. We start with subsetting all of them to the `r dim(NHEFS.3.com)[1]` participants that were common to the all three NHEFS data sets.

```{r}

NHEFS.1.sub  <- NHEFS.1 |> filter(ssn %in% ssn_keep)
NHEFS.2.sub  <- NHEFS.2 |> filter(ssn %in% ssn_keep)
NHEFS.3.sub  <- NHEFS.3.com

```

Now we further subset them to the complete case participants and keep the participants which has complete cases along all the three NHEFS data.

\textbf{Again, probably we could have done this more efficiently but for the sake of time and computation burden we are doing this only.}

```{r}

vars_cont <- c("age", "height", "weight")
vars_cat <- c("sex", "vital.st", "race", "mar.st", "gen.hlth")

ssn_1 <- NHEFS.1.sub |>
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |>
  filter(complete.cases(across(-ssn))) |>
  pull(ssn)


ssn_2 <- NHEFS.2.sub |>
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |>
  filter(complete.cases(across(-ssn))) |>
  pull(ssn)

ssn_3 <- NHEFS.3.sub |>
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |>
  filter(complete.cases(across(-ssn))) |>
  pull(ssn)

ssn_common <- Reduce(intersect, list(ssn_1, ssn_2, ssn_3))

length(ssn_common)

NHEFS.1.sub <- NHEFS.1.sub |> filter(ssn %in% ssn_common) |> 
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |> 
  mutate(across(any_of(vars_cat), as.factor))
NHEFS.2.sub <- NHEFS.2.sub |> filter(ssn %in% ssn_common) |> 
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |> 
  mutate(across(any_of(vars_cat), as.factor))
NHEFS.3.sub <- NHEFS.3.sub |> filter(ssn %in% ssn_common) |> 
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_cont), any_of(vars_cat)) |> 
  mutate(across(any_of(vars_cat), as.factor))

```

We see that there are still `r length(ssn_common)` participants in the three NHEFS data sets which is still enough. We go ahead and fit the data sets with all the four methods.

<!-- ===================================================================== -->
<!-- NHEFS.01 data -->

## Fitting for NHEFS.01 data set

```{r}

cur.df <- NHEFS.1.sub

## =========== K-means clustering ===========

one_level_vars <- cur.df |> select(-ssn) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), n_distinct)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_levels") |>
  filter(n_levels <= 1) |> pull(variable)

cur.df_km <- cur.df |>
  select(-all_of(one_level_vars))

X_base <- model.matrix(~ . - ssn - 1, data = cur.df_km)
X_base_scaled <- scale(X_base)

K_choose <- 6

set.seed(2025)
km_final <- kmeans(X_base_scaled, centers = K_choose, nstart = 100)

cur.df <- cur.df |> mutate(cluster_km = factor(km_final$cluster))

## =========== Bayesian GMM clustering ===========

N <- nrow(X_base_scaled)
D <- ncol(X_base_scaled)
K <- K_choose

bgmm_data <- list(N = N, D = D, K = K, X = X_base_scaled)

# set.seed(100)
# bgmm_fit.1 <- stan(
#   model_code = bgmm_stan_code,
#   data       = bgmm_data,
#   iter       = 2000,
#   warmup     = 1000,
#   chains     = 1,
#   cores      = detectCores(),
#   seed       = 100
# )
# 
# theta_hat <- colMeans(as.data.frame(extract(bgmm_fit.1, "theta")$theta))
# mu_hat    <- apply(extract(bgmm_fit.1, "mu")$mu,    c(2, 3), mean)
# sigma_hat <- apply(extract(bgmm_fit.1, "sigma")$sigma, c(2, 3), mean)
# 
# bgmm_list.1 <- list(theta_hat, mu_hat, sigma_hat)
# 
# save(bgmm_list.1, file = "fit.bgmm.1.Rdata")

load("fit.bgmm.1.Rdata")

theta_hat <- bgmm_list.1[[1]]
mu_hat    <- bgmm_list.1[[2]]
sigma_hat <- bgmm_list.1[[3]]

log_resp <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = N, ncol = K)

for (n in 1:N) {
  for (k in 1:K) {
    lp <- log(theta_hat[k])
    for (d in 1:D) {
      lp <- lp + dnorm(X_base_scaled[n, d], mean = mu_hat[k, d],
                       sd   = sigma_hat[k, d], log  = TRUE)
    }
    log_resp[n, k] <- lp
  }
}

resp <- exp(log_resp - apply(log_resp, 1, max))
resp <- resp / rowSums(resp)

cluster_bgmm <- max.col(resp)     

cur.df$cluster_bgmm <- factor(cluster_bgmm)

## =========== CLAMR clustering ===========

mr_vars <- vars_cont
cur.df_clamr <- cur.df |> select(ssn, all_of(mr_vars))

L <- 3

mr_bounds <- lapply(mr_vars, function(v) {
  x <- cur.df_clamr[[v]]
  qs <- quantile(x, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
  as.numeric(qs)
})
names(mr_bounds) <- mr_vars

z975 <- qnorm(0.975)

mr_mid <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(mr_vars), ncol = L)
mr_sd  <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(mr_vars), ncol = L)

for (j in seq_along(mr_vars)) {
  b <- mr_bounds[[j]]
  for (l in 1:L) {
    a_l <- b[l]
    b_l <- b[l + 1]
    mr_mid[j, l] <- (a_l + b_l) / 2
    mr_sd[j, l]  <- (b_l - a_l) / (2 * z975)  
  }
}

alpha_mr <- matrix(1, nrow = length(mr_vars), ncol = L)

X_clamr <- as.matrix(cur.df_clamr[, mr_vars])

N <- nrow(X_clamr)
D <- ncol(X_clamr)
K <- K_choose

clamr_data <- list(N = N, D = D, K = K, L = L, X = X_clamr, mr_mid  = mr_mid, 
                   mr_sd   = mr_sd, alpha_mr = alpha_mr)

# set.seed(100)
# clamr_fit.1 <- stan(
#   model_code = clamr_stan_code,
#   data       = clamr_data,
#   iter       = 2000,
#   warmup     = 1000,
#   chains     = 1,
#   cores      = detectCores(),
#   seed       = 100
# )
# 
# post <- extract(clamr_fit.1)
# 
# theta_hat <- colMeans(post$theta)                   
# mu_hat    <- apply(post$mu, c(2, 3), mean)       
# sigma_hat <- apply(post$sigma, c(2, 3), mean) 
# 
# clamr_list.1 <- list(theta_hat, mu_hat, sigma_hat)
# 
# save(clamr_list.1, file = "fit.clamr.1.Rdata")

load("fit.clamr.1.Rdata")

theta_hat <- clamr_list.1[[1]]
mu_hat    <- clamr_list.1[[2]]
sigma_hat <- clamr_list.1[[3]]

log_resp <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = N, ncol = K)

for (n in 1:N) {
  for (k in 1:K) {
    lp <- log(theta_hat[k])
    for (d in 1:D) {
      lp <- lp + dnorm(X_clamr[n, d], mean = mu_hat[k, d],
                       sd   = sigma_hat[k, d], log  = TRUE)
    }
    log_resp[n, k] <- lp
  }
}

resp <- exp(log_resp - apply(log_resp, 1, max))
resp <- resp / rowSums(resp)

cluster_clamr <- max.col(resp)   
cur.df$cluster_clamr <- factor(cluster_clamr)

## =========== Bayesian pyramid clustering ===========

vars_pyr <- vars_cat

cur.df_pyr <- cur.df |>
  select(ssn, any_of(vars_pyr)) |> 
  mutate(across(all_of(vars_pyr), ~ as.integer(factor(.))))

Y_cat <- as.matrix(cur.df_pyr[, vars_pyr])

N <- nrow(Y_cat)
P <- ncol(Y_cat)
C <- apply(Y_cat, 2, max)
C_max <- max(C)
K_pyr <- K_choose

pyr_data <- list(N = N, P = P, K = K_pyr, C_max = C_max, Y = Y_cat)

# set.seed(100)
# pyr_fit.1 <- stan(
#   model_code = pyramid_stan_code,
#   data       = pyr_data,
#   iter       = 2000,
#   warmup     = 1000,
#   chains     = 1,
#   cores      = detectCores(),
#   seed       = 100
# )
# 
# post <- extract(pyr_fit.1)
# 
# theta_hat <- colMeans(post$theta)
# phi_array <- post$phi
# phi_hat <- apply(phi_array, c(2, 3, 4), mean)
# 
# pyr_list.1 <- list(theta_hat, phi_hat)
# 
# save(pyr_list.1, file = "fit.pyr.1.Rdata")

load("fit.pyr.1.Rdata")

theta_hat <- pyr_list.1[[1]]
phi_hat <- pyr_list.1[[2]]

log_resp_pyr <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = N, ncol = K_pyr)

for (n in 1:N) {
  for (k in 1:K_pyr) {
    lp <- log(theta_hat[k])
    for (p in 1:P) {
      cat_idx <- Y_cat[n, p]    # in 1..C_max
      lp <- lp + log(phi_hat[k, p, cat_idx])
    }
    log_resp_pyr[n, k] <- lp
  }
}

resp_pyr <- exp(log_resp_pyr - apply(log_resp_pyr, 1, max))
resp_pyr <- resp_pyr / rowSums(resp_pyr)

cluster_pyr <- max.col(resp_pyr)
cur.df$cluster_pyr <- factor(cluster_pyr)

## ================

NHEFS.1.sub <- cur.df

```

# Similarity between clusters accross waves

To answer this question, we calculate ARI for each pair of NHEFS waves for all the clustering methods. 

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

waves <- list(NHEFS.1 = NHEFS.1.sub,
              NHEFS.2 = NHEFS.2.sub,
              NHEFS.3 = NHEFS.3.sub)

methods <- c("cluster_km", "cluster_bgmm", "cluster_clamr", "cluster_pyr")

pairs   <- list(c("NHEFS.1", "NHEFS.2"),
                c("NHEFS.1", "NHEFS.3"),
                c("NHEFS.2", "NHEFS.3"))

get_ari <- function(df1, df2, colname) {
  tmp <- inner_join(
    df1 %>% 
      select(ssn, cl1 = !!sym(colname)),
    df2 %>%
      select(ssn, cl2 = !!sym(colname)),
    by = "ssn"
    )
  adjustedRandIndex(tmp$cl1, tmp$cl2)
}

ari_waves <- purrr::map_dfr(methods, function(m) {
  purrr::map_dfr(pairs, function(p) {
    df1 <- waves[[p[1]]]
    df2 <- waves[[p[2]]]
    tibble(method = m, wave1 = p[1], wave2 = p[2], 
           ARI = get_ari(df1, df2, m))
  })
})

knitr::kable(ari_waves, caption = "Adjusted Rand indices comparing 
             clusterings across NHEFS waves.")

```

The above table reports ARIs comparing the cluster assignments for the same individuals across the three NHEFS waves. Overall, the values are well above zero for all methods, indicating that the basic clustering structure is reasonably stable over time.  

For k--means, the ARI between W1 and W2 is high (0.80), but drops to about 0.55 for comparisons involving W3, suggesting that the baseline clusters are largely preserved at the first follow--up but begin to diverge more by the second follow--up.

The BGMM exhibits the greatest temporal stability: ARIs of 0.76 (W1 vs W2) and 0.76 (W1 vs W3) already indicate strong agreement, and the ARI of 0.97 between W2 and W3 implies that the mixture model produces almost identical clusterings at the two later waves.  

In contrast, the CLAMR clusterings are less stable across time, with only modest agreement between W1 and W2 (0.38) and between W1 and W3 (0.40), although the ARI between W2 and W3 (0.71) still indicates substantial similarity once the model has been refit on the follow--up data.

The Bayesian Pyramids solution lies between these extremes, with ARIs ranging from about 0.70 (W1 vs W3) to 0.81 (W2 vs W3), reflecting a moderately high degree of persistence in its latent classes.  

Taken together, these results suggest that all methods capture underlying phenotypes that are reasonably consistent across waves, with BGMM providing the most stable cluster assignments and CLAMR being the most sensitive to changes in the data over time.

# Analysis of NHEFS.1 data set similar to NHANES.1 data set

We just do the analysis for the NHEFS.1 data set. The other one can be done very similarly, with just replacing \texttt{NHEFS.1.sub} by \texttt{NHEFS.2.sub} or \texttt{NHEFS.3.sub} in the following code chunk.
