```{r}
df.cur.nhefs <- NHEFS.1.sub
```

## Finding similarities between clustering procedures

We calculate the similarities between the clusters by calculating the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) using the \texttt{adjustedRandIndex()} function from the \texttt{hclust} package.

```{r}

df_clust <- df.cur.nhefs

# Calculating ARIs
(ari_km_bgmm    <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_km,
                                     df_clust$cluster_bgmm))
(ari_km_clamr   <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_km,
                                     df_clust$cluster_clamr))
(ari_km_pyr     <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_km,
                                     df_clust$cluster_pyr))
(ari_bgmm_clamr <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_bgmm,
                                     df_clust$cluster_clamr))
(ari_bgmm_pyr   <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_bgmm,
                                     df_clust$cluster_pyr))
(ari_clamr_pyr  <- adjustedRandIndex(df_clust$cluster_clamr, 
                                     df_clust$cluster_pyr))

```

We can see that for the NHEFS.1 data set, the ARI between k-means clustering and the Bayesian GMM clustering are pretty high. The others are still low, but higher than the NHANES data set.

## Most influencial feature for determining the clustering

We again implement the testing set up we described for the NHANES.1 data set to obtain the rank for the most influential variables for each clustering methods.

```{r}

# defining a function

cluster_var_importance <- function(df, cluster_var, cont_vars, cat_vars) {
  cl <- df[[cluster_var]]
  
  # continuous: ANOVA F-stat
  cont_res <- map_dfr(cont_vars, function(v) {
    x <- df[[v]]
    idx <- complete.cases(cl, x)
    if (length(unique(cl[idx])) < 2) return(NULL)
    fit <- lm(x[idx] ~ cl[idx])
    aov_tab <- anova(fit)
    tibble(
      variable = v,
      type     = "continuous",
      stat     = aov_tab$`F value`[1]
    )
  })
  
  # categorical: chi-square
  cat_res <- map_dfr(cat_vars, function(v) {
    x <- df[[v]]
    idx <- complete.cases(cl, x)
    tab <- table(cl[idx], x[idx])
    if (any(dim(tab) < 2)) return(NULL)
    chi <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
    tibble(
      variable = v,
      type     = "categorical",
      stat     = unname(chi$statistic)
    )
  })
  
  bind_rows(cont_res, cat_res) |>
    arrange(desc(stat))
}

df_inf.feat <- df.cur.nhefs
vars_cont <- c("age", "height", "weight")
vars_cat <- c("sex", "vital.st", "race", "mar.st", "gen.hlth")

imp_km    <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_km",    
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat) 
imp_bgmm  <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_bgmm",  
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat)
imp_clamr <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_clamr", 
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat)
imp_pyr   <- cluster_var_importance(df_inf.feat, "cluster_pyr",   
                                    vars_cont, vars_cat)

(var_rank_tbl <- tibble(Rank  = 1:7, km = imp_km$variable,
                       bgmm  = imp_km$variable, clamr = imp_clamr$variable, 
                       pyr   = imp_pyr$variable))

```

The above table shows the ranking of baseline variables by their association with cluster membership for the four methods applied to the NHEFS.1 data.  Overall, the rankings are broadly consistent.  For k--means and the BGMM, \texttt{mar.st} (marital status) and \texttt{race} occupy the top two positions, followed by \texttt{gen.hlth} and \texttt{sex}.  Thus, social and demographic characteristics form the primary axes along which these methods partition the population, with general health and sex providing secondary refinement within those groups.  CLAMR places \texttt{sex} and \texttt{age} at the top of the list, with \texttt{height} and \texttt{weight} close behind, reflecting its stronger emphasis on continuous clinical variables; marital status and general health move slightly lower in its ranking.  The Bayesian Pyramids model, which works directly with categorical structure, again highlights \texttt{mar.st}, \texttt{sex}, and \texttt{gen.hlth} among the most important features, with \texttt{race}, \texttt{height}, \texttt{weight}, and \texttt{age} occupying the middle and lower ranks.  Taken together, these results indicate that marital status, race, general health, and sex are the key drivers of cluster formation in NHEFS.1, while age and anthropometric measures (height and weight) play a consistent but somewhat less dominant role, except in CLAMR where they are given greater prominence.

## Relationship between baseline clusters and subsequent mortality

Very unfortunately, all the `r nrow(NHEFS.1.sub)` participants we selected none of them are dead in any of the waves. So we can't really compare the mortality with the clustering. But we will provide a review of the clusters obtained.

Again, let's focus on the CLAMR clustering and plot the similar plots as NHANES.1.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

df.plot.cont <- df.cur.nhefs |> 
  pivot_longer( cols = c(age, height, weight),
                names_to  = "variable",
                values_to = "value") |> 
  mutate(cluster_clamr = paste0("Cluster: ", cluster_clamr))

ggplot(df.plot.cont, aes(x = variable, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster_clamr, scales = "free_y") +
  labs( x = "CLAMR cluster variables", y = "Value",
    title = "Distribution of continuous variable by CLAMR cluster") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7}

cat_vars <- c("gen.hlth", "race", "mar.st", "sex")

df.plot.cat <- df.cur.nhefs |> pivot_longer(all_of(cat_vars),
                                             names_to = "variable",
                                             values_to = "level")

cat_props <- df.plot.cat |>
  group_by(cluster_clamr, variable, level) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |> 
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))) |> 
  mutate(cluster_clamr = paste0("Cluster: ", cluster_clamr))

ggplot(cat_props, aes(x = variable, y = prop, fill = level)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  facet_wrap( ~ cluster_clamr) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Baseline categorical variable",
       y = "Proportion within cluster", fill = "Category",
       title = "Distribution of categorical variable by CLAMR cluster",
       subtitle = "With mortality risk") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

The CLAMR model partitions the NHEFS.1 cohort into six clusters that differ systematically in anthropometric measurements and in the distributions of key categorical covariates.  The continuous--variable plot shows that clusters~3 and~5 contain the heaviest individuals: both clusters have markedly higher weights than the remaining clusters, with cluster~3 combining high weight with relatively greater height, and cluster~5 representing a shorter but particularly heavy group.  Clusters~1 and~4 have intermediate body size, with moderate weights and heights, whereas cluster~2 is characterised by taller but comparatively lean individuals.  Cluster~6 contains subjects with relatively lower weight and more concentrated height and age distributions, suggesting a leaner phenotype.

The categorical summaries indicate that the clusters also differ in their composition with respect to general health, marital status, race, and sex. Within each cluster the bars for \texttt{gen.hlth} and \texttt{mar.st} reveal distinct mixtures of response categories, with some clusters (e.g.\ clusters~4 and~5) showing a greater representation of non–reference categories, and others (notably clusters~2 and~6) being dominated by the reference levels. Race and sex also vary by cluster, although more moderately: certain clusters are predominantly one sex or racial category, whereas others exhibit a more balanced mix.  Taken together, these patterns suggest that the CLAMR algorithm has identified six clinically interpretable phenotypes in NHEFS.1, defined by joint differences in age, body size, self–reported health, and basic sociodemographic characteristics, rather than by a single variable alone.

\newpage
## Challenges in describing how clustering changes over time

There are several conceptual and practical challenges in describing how clustering evolves across the waves.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Lack of a natural cluster identity over time.}
  Clustering is an unsupervised task, so cluster labels are arbitrary at each wave.  Even when two clustering are very similar, there is no canonical one--to--one correspondence between labels at different waves.  Clusters may also split and merge across waves.  This complicates statements such as 'cluster~3 becomes cluster~5', because such statements depend on an \emph{ad hoc} label--matching rule.  The literature on label switching and post hoc relabeling in mixture models offers ways to define reasonable mappings, but none provides a unique notion of `the same cluster over time'.

  \item \textbf{Changing marginal distributions and covariate sets.}
  As the cohort ages, the marginal distributions of key variables (age, weight, comorbidities, general health) change substantially, and some variables are only measured or defined in certain waves.  A cluster of `older, heavy, poor--health' individuals at any wave may correspond to quite different absolute levels of age and weight by another wave.  Thus, equality of clusters across time is ill defined unless one explicitly decides whether clusters are defined relative to the current marginal distribution or on an absolute scale.  Existing work on time--varying or dynamic mixture models (e.g.\ mixtures with time--indexed parameters, dependent Dirichlet processes) attempts to encode smooth evolution of cluster parameters, but implementing such models in high dimension remains challenging.

  \item \textbf{Subject movement and cluster transitions.}
  Individuals are not static. They can improve or worsen in health, change behaviors (smoking, alcohol), or receive new diagnoses.  Even if the \emph{cluster definitions} were perfectly stable over time, the proportion of subjects moving between clusters may be substantial.  Describing this requires some notion of a transition matrix or latent Markov structure (latent transition analysis, hidden Markov models with mixture emission distributions, growth mixture models), rather than simply comparing cross--sectional clustering at each wave.  The methods used here (separate clustering by wave) ignore this dynamic structure, so any description of 'cluster evolution' is inherently approximate.

  \item \textbf{Missing data and informative dropout.}
  In longitudinal health studies, missingness is almost never completely at random.  In NHEFS, missingness and loss to follow--up are strongly related to age, general health, and comorbidities, and thus to cluster membership itself.  High--risk individuals may die or drop out, so the composition of clusters among survivors at later waves is a biased version of the original population.  This makes it difficult to distinguish true changes in cluster structure from artefacts induced by informative dropout.  Joint models for longitudinal and survival data, pattern--mixture models, and selection models address aspects of this problem, but incorporating them into complex clustering frameworks (particularly the more elaborate Bayesian models) is still an active research area.

  \item \textbf{Model choice and uncertainty in the number of clusters.}
  In practice we fixed the number of clusters $K$ for each method, but the `true' number of clusters, if such a notion exists, may itself change over time.  Moreover, different methods favour different effective numbers of clusters (e.g.\ BGMM selecting fewer active components than CLAMR).  This model uncertainty is not typically propagated into statements about temporal change.  Bayesian nonparametric mixture models or model--averaging approaches can in principle account for uncertainty in $K$, but do not fully solve the interpretational difficulty of saying how an evolving random partition changes across time.
\end{enumerate}

In summary, the existing literature provides tools for (i) aligning clusters between time points (relabeling / optimal matching), (ii) explicitly modelling time--varying mixture parameters (dynamic mixtures, dependent Dirichlet processes), and (iii) modelling transition behaviour (latent Markov and growth mixture models).  However, fully coherent longitudinal clustering that jointly handles time evolution, missingness, and model uncertainty remains difficult, and most applied analyses rely on simpler comparisons of cross--sectional clusterings at each wave, supplemented by descriptive summaries of how cluster profiles and sizes change over time.

\newpage

## Do meaningful clusters exist in these data?

Several pieces of evidence suggest that the clusters we obtain are
substantively meaningful rather than mere artefacts of the algorithms.

\begin{itemize}

  \item \textbf{Stable phenotypic interpretation.}
  For each method, cluster profiles in terms of age, height, weight, general health, marital status, and comorbidity history show clear and interpretable patterns.  Across waves and methods, we consistently see clusters characterised by older age, higher body weight, and poorer self--reported health, as well as clusters of younger, lighter, healthier individuals. These patterns are robust to the choice of clustering algorithm and persist when the models are refit on follow--up waves, suggesting that the methods are capturing underlying health phenotypes rather than idiosyncratic noise.

  \item \textbf{Predictive value for mortality.}
  Baseline clusters are strongly associated with subsequent mortality in the NHEFS data.  For example, under the CLAMR model applied to NHANES I, high--risk clusters (notably cluster~5, and to a lesser extent clusters~3 and~4) have much higher cumulative mortality than low--risk clusters~2 and~6, even after several years of follow--up.  Similar patterns are observed for the other methods: clusters defined by older age and poor general health exhibit substantially higher mortality than clusters of younger, healthier subjects.  The fact that unsupervised clusters formed without using outcome information nonetheless show strong associations with a hard clinical endpoint provides compelling evidence that the clusters are clinically meaningful.

  \item \textbf{Temporal persistence of cluster structure.}
  While individual membership changes over time, the ARIs comparing clusterings across waves are generally well above zero, especially for BGMM and Pyramids (e.g.\ ARIs around $0.7$--$0.97$ between W1, W2 and W3).  Moreover, the high--risk and low--risk phenotypes identified at baseline remain visible in later waves: later--wave clusters with the worst general health and highest body weight tend to correspond to those with the highest observed mortality.  This temporal persistence is difficult to explain if the clusters were purely artefactual.

\end{itemize}

On the other hand, the evidence is not perfectly decisive.  ARIs between methods and waves are far from one, indicating substantial uncertainty in cluster membership; the number of clusters is chosen rather than inferred from first principles and clustering in moderate dimensions with large sample sizes can always find some structure, even in nearly homogeneous data.  Thus, we should view the clusters as \emph{useful low--dimensional summaries} that capture major gradients in age, body size, and health status, rather than as uniquely defined, sharply separated subpopulations.

Overall, however, the combination of (i) clear and interpretable differences in baseline characteristics, (ii) strong associations with subsequent mortality, and (iii) persistence of cluster profiles over time supports the conclusion that meaningful clusters do exist in these data and that they correspond to clinically relevant risk strata in the NHEFS cohort.
